claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite with interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
A uniform 5–10 nm Ni coating is to be deposited on W particle or ligament surfaces before consolidation.
The coated composite is to be spark-plasma-sintered at approximately 1000°C and 50 MPa for 10 minutes under high vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Spark plasma sintering of Ni-coated W surfaces will form an interfacial Ni-rich layer.
The Ni-rich layer will promote strong bonding between W and Cu.
The Ni-rich layer will act as an effective diffusion barrier.
During spark plasma sintering, Ni will locally alloy with both W and Cu to create a stable W–Ni–Cu interlayer.
The W–Ni–Cu interlayer will reduce interfacial energy.
The W–Ni–Cu interlayer will limit excessive interdiffusion.
The W–Ni–Cu interlayer will prevent or reduce void nucleation and preserve a coherent interface during cyclic heat and irradiation exposure.
The Ni-coated composite will have fewer interfacial voids than an otherwise identically processed uncoated composite.
The Ni-coated composite will exhibit less phase separation than the uncoated composite.
Reduced void formation and phase separation will produce higher thermal conductivity in the Ni-coated composite than in the uncoated composite.
An uncoated W–Cu composite typically develops interfacial voids and phase separation under similar processing and service conditions.
Interfacial voids and phase separation in the uncoated composite lead to inferior thermal conductivity.
The proposed benefits are expected near 1000°C, 50 MPa, and short SPS dwell times and during service involving cyclic heat transfer and irradiation.
Changes in Ni coating thickness, sintering temperature, or pressure may alter the robustness of the interfacial layer.
